title: How do you answer "Tell me about a time you failed" without hurting your chances?
description: How to answer the failure question in consulting interviews honestly, with weak and strong example answers and the mistakes to avoid.
hook: This question makes people nervous, so many dodge it with a disguised strength. Interviewers can tell, and it costs trust. A real failure, told well, is far more convincing.
body:
The question

Tell me about a time you failed.

A weak answer

I think my biggest failure is that I sometimes work too hard and take on too much, so I had to learn to delegate.

Why it falls short: It is not a failure; it is a disguised strength. It sounds rehearsed and avoids the question.

A strong answer

In my first job I launched a customer survey without testing it with a small group first. Two of the questions were confusing, so a third of the answers were unusable and we had to rerun it, delaying a decision by a month. It was my call to skip the pilot to save time. Since then I always test anything customer-facing with five or six people first. On my next project that pilot caught a pricing error before launch.

Why it works: A real mistake with real consequences, clear ownership, and a specific change in behaviour with evidence that it worked.

Make it your own

Copy the shape of the strong answer, not its words. Write your own version of "Tell me about a time you failed" in five or six sentences from a real moment, then say it aloud until it sounds natural.

Make the consequence and the correction concrete

The failure question is not an invitation to present a disguised strength. Choose a real mistake you own, ideally one where the cost was visible but manageable, and explain the action you took afterwards. An interviewer should hear accountability rather than an excuse.

An illustrative answer: "I led a pilot to introduce a new reporting dashboard. I assumed the team would adopt it because the underlying metrics were useful, so I spent most of the first month building features and very little time observing how people made decisions. Only 40% of the intended users used it weekly against our 70% goal. After interviewing six colleagues, I realised the dashboard duplicated an existing morning report and omitted the one breakdown managers needed. I simplified the view, changed the launch plan and introduced the revised tool through existing team meetings. In the following pilot, weekly usage reached 72%. The mistake was treating technical completion as proof of user value." The figures are hypothetical; use your actual evidence.

The learning is credible because the behaviour changed: the candidate began testing workflows before investing in more features. Do not conclude with "I now work harder" or "I am a perfectionist". Those do not identify a repeatable correction.

A follow-up interviewer may ask why the team did not catch the problem earlier. State your responsibility plainly, including any warning signs you missed. If the eventual outcome improved, still acknowledge the wasted time, missed adoption or cost of the original error.
